content: Countries within the six WHO regions are provided with recommendations tailored to regional immunization priorities and strategies. These recommendations are informed by regional epidemiological and social considerations. National Immunization Technical Advisory Groups (NITAGs) are multidisciplinary panels of national experts. They deliver evidence-based recommendations to policymakers and immunization program managers to guide vaccination strategies. The WHO Steering Group on Vaccination Policy Guidance is composed of senior WHO staff nominated by the IVB (Immunization, Vaccines, and Biologicals) director. This internal mechanism ensures critical oversight in the development of WHO vaccine position papers, which articulate WHO’s immunization policies and strategic advice. However, the Steering Group does not participate in the work of the SAGE (Strategic Advisory Group of Experts) working group or SAGE itself. Instead, it advises on the need to update vaccine position papers or other vaccination policy guidance documents. WHO may engage external contractors with the necessary expertise and no conflicts of interest to compile evidence that supports SAGE’s recommendations. These contractors may conduct systematic reviews of the literature, appraise available evidence, or develop mathematical models to assess the impact or cost-effectiveness of interventions. All external contractors must adhere to the WHO Code of Conduct for Responsible Research. The Product Development for Vaccines Advisory Committee (PDVAC) is an independent WHO expert group that advises on vaccine and monoclonal antibody product development, manufacturing, and delivery technologies for priority infectious diseases. PDVAC focuses on diseases with significant burdens in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), especially where no vaccines currently exist but where product development is underway. It also addresses technologies that could expedite vaccine availability and access in LMICs. PDVAC may also prioritize improving existing vaccines, including those based on novel manufacturing technologies or innovative delivery approaches. Its mission is to accelerate the development of urgently needed vaccines and technologies, ensuring they are appropriately targeted for use in LMICs. PDVAC convenes stakeholders across various sectors to coordinate and align product development strategies for priority vaccines and technologies. It also discusses novel regulatory pathways and aspects that may inform vaccine value assessments. PDVAC provides guidance on preferred product characteristics, technical R&D roadmaps, and evidence considerations for vaccine policy, as well as data needs to support policy decisions. SAGE working groups and recommendations build upon these efforts as vaccine candidates progress toward regulatory approval. Throughout the year, the SAGE secretariat monitors the global vaccine landscape, tracks data from vaccine monitoring and evaluation systems, and collects informal requests for SAGE advice. These requests may originate from within or outside WHO, including regional offices, technical partners, stakeholders, SAGE members, and the SAGE steering group. Proposed topics are assessed for their suitability for SAGE advice. Annually, potential SAGE topics are reviewed by the SAGE secretariat, IVB management, and the SAGE chair. The IVB director determines which topics will be considered for SAGE advice within the next 12–24 months, based on WHO priorities and resources. These topics form the SAGE work plan, which is published on the SAGE website. Three months before each SAGE meeting, the agenda is determined by IVB senior management in consultation with the SAGE secretariat and chair. The agenda is based on the annual work plan and considers the preparatory work and evidence synthesis required for SAGE deliberations. WHO retains the right to add topics to the agenda at short notice, such as during health emergencies. SAGE meetings occur biannually and are structured into open and closed sessions. Open plenary sessions allow for the exchange of non-confidential information and technical input from experts. Closed sessions are reserved for SAGE members and the WHO Secretariat to finalize recommendations. Recommendations are reached by consensus, with a quorum of two-thirds of members present. If consensus cannot be reached, additional information is sought, and the issue is revisited at a later meeting. In exceptional circumstances, such as during a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC), extraordinary SAGE meetings may be convened to provide immediate advice and guidance. Following SAGE meetings, the SAGE chair presents a report to the WHO Director-General or delegate, summarizing the main outcomes and recommendations. Only after this presentation are recommendations publicly communicated. SAGE recommendations are advisory, and WHO retains full control over subsequent decisions or actions. If WHO disagrees with SAGE’s advice, any divergent views will be transparently documented in the final meeting report. All SAGE-related materials, including terms of reference, member compositions, meeting materials, and vaccine position papers, are publicly available on the WHO SAGE website. High-level summaries of deliberations are released shortly after meetings, followed by comprehensive reports published in the WHO Weekly Epidemiological Record approximately six weeks later. Official WHO advice resulting in vaccination policy updates is reflected in vaccine position papers published about three months after the respective meeting. To ensure objectivity and independence, WHO requires experts serving in advisory roles to disclose any potential or perceived conflicts of interest. A conflict of interest is defined as any financial or intellectual interest that may affect, or be perceived to affect, an individual’s objectivity in providing advice to WHO. Declared interests are assessed on a case-by-case basis by the SAGE secretariat and, if necessary, the WHO Office of Compliance, Risk Management, and Ethics. Final decisions are made by WHO. Experts with significant conflicts may be excluded from discussions or recommendation-making. Summarized reported interests and their implications are publicly disclosed on the SAGE website for transparency. The funding for WHO policy development processes is designed to safeguard the independence of involved parties and ensure that funders do not influence content or recommendations. Funding sources include assessed contributions (country membership dues) and voluntary contributions from Member States, UN organizations, intergovernmental organizations, philanthropic foundations, the private sector, and other sources. Activities of the SAGE secretariat, SAGE, and its working groups may be funded through these contributions, following careful evaluation and compliance with WHO’s Framework of Engagement with non-State actors (FENSA). The development of WHO vaccine and immunization-related recommendations follows rigorous processes and methods outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development. Policy questions addressed by SAGE are often broad and overarching, such as whether a specific vaccine should be introduced into routine immunization programs. These questions are structured into specific elements using the PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome) model to guide evidence collection and assessment. Systematic reviews of literature are conducted to support evidence-based practices and healthcare decisions. These reviews involve comprehensive and structured search processes, conducted independently with clearly formulated research questions.
